form: While preparing a Lushootseed Reader, we came across two difficult sentences in a fascinating text on how to play the Bone Game, sləhal. The sentences are:
kʷaʔ ləcux̌əčadadid dxʷʔal tiʔəʔ sʔacuss (h)əlgʷəʔ dəxʷx̌əbil ʔə tiʔəʔ.
Instead he is sending-his-power-of-thought-over-them to their faces so that these (opponents) become heavy.
x̌əčadadid tiʔəʔ stabtablax̌əd ʔə tiʔəʔ də(xʷ)xʷak̓ʷils, dəxʷgʷəƛ̓əlads ʔə tiʔəʔ sudᶻigʷicuts.
He directs-his-thoughts to the arms of these (opponents) so that they become tired, so that they stop their back-and-forth-movement.
Students are troubled by the fact that the verb in dəxʷ- clause (1) does not have an -s suffix while in clause (2) it does:
... dəxʷx̌əbil ʔə tiʔəʔ ...
gloss: so that they become heavy.

form: ... dəxʷgʷəƛ̓əlads ʔə tiʔəʔ sudᶻigʷicuts. ...
gloss: so that they stop their swaying back and forth.

form: Both sentences were grammatical, but why?
The name Lushootseed is now being used instead of Puget Salish. Lushootseed is based upon the Indian name for the language, dxʷləšucid.

The problem lies with the several uses of ʔə. Phrases beginning with this particle look the same but fit into the rest of the sentence in several different ways. Some other Salish languages have a similar ʔə word, so its use in Lushootseed and the explanation for the difference above may have general interest.
The ʔə in Lushootseed links six different types of phrase and clause to the rest in the sentence. These six are:
I Phrases of manner and instrument:
ʔuʔəɬəd ʔə tə qa.
gloss: He ate a lot.

form: ʔuyayus ʔə tə tib.
gloss: He worked hard.

form: ʔupusud ʔə tə č̓ƛ̓aʔ.
gloss: He threw a rock at someone. (He threw at someone with a rock.)

form: II Phrases expressing patient of verbs that do not have a transitive suffix:
ʔugʷəč̓ᵊb ʔə ti x̌ʷubt.
gloss: He looked for the paddle.

form: ʔugʷəč̓ᵊd ti x̌ʷubt.
gloss: He looked for the paddle.

form: The - d is a transitive suffix; therefore no ʔə precedes ti x̌ʷubt.
ʔut̓əqalikʷ ʔə tə səpləl.
gloss: She made bread.

form: III Phrases expressing agent of "passive" verbs:
ʔukʷaxʷatᵊb ʔə tsi dsqa tsiʔiɬ sk̓ʷuyčəɬ.
gloss: My older sister helped our mother.

form: ʔux̌əƛ̓tᵊb ʔə tə sqʷəbayʔ.
gloss: A dog bit someone.

form: Similar to ʔə is the word ʔal which introduces phrases of location and time. Often, ʔə replaces ʔal in both of these, especially in phrases of location.
The term passive is not particularly appropriate for Lushootseed. More precisely, we mean those verbs that end with a transitive suffix plus {b}.
IV Phrases following benefactive verbs that express the item transferred:
ʔutagʷyic tsiʔiɬ ʔə tiʔəʔ x̌aw̓s qʷ(ə)ɬiʔšəd.
gloss: She bought me a new (pair of) shoes.

form: ʔuqadayic tiʔiɬ ʔə ti x̌ʷubt.
gloss: He stole the paddle from me.

form: ʔuɬilc tsiʔiɬ sɬadəyʔ ʔə tə səpləl.
gloss: That woman gave me some bread.

form: V Phrases expressing possessor:
ti sqʷəbayʔ ʔə tiʔiɬ stubš.
gloss: That man's dog. (The dog of that man.)

form: tə səpləl ʔə tsi dsk̓ʷuy.
gloss: My mother's bread. (Bread of my mother.)

form: ti sqʷəbayʔs
gloss: his dog

form: tə səpləls
gloss: her bread

form: VI Subordinate clauses expressing manner, means, (or sometimes location (instead of ʔal). This is an extension of I.)
ʔukʷaxʷatᵊb ʔə tsi dsqa ʔə ti sut̓əqalikʷs.
gloss: My older sister helped with her (someone else's) bread-making.

form: ʔušudub ʔə tə sqʷəbayʔ ʔə ti suʔigʷəɬs.
gloss: A dog saw it climb (the tree).

form: Here benefactive is a cover term designating verbs having the secondary suffix -yi- and verbs of giving like ɬil-. The action may be to one's detriment (cf. 12) as well as benefit.

It may well be that, from the Lushootseed point of view, phrases I, II, and IV state the same type of information and are grammatically equivalent. It would be interesting to compare the grammatical formations that related languages use to express these concepts. Do any other Salish languages convey all of these concepts with the same grammatical structures as does Lushootseed?

Subordinate clauses have one characteristic that bears upon the problem, viz., the agent of the verb is expressed by the same affixes that denote possession. For third person that affix is the suffix -s; and like possessive constructions, the -s can be replaced by an ʔə phrase. (Compare (16) and (17) with (14) and (15).) Therefore, it is possible to make explicit who was helped with the bread-making in (18) and who (or what) climbed (the tree) in (19) by replacing -s with ʔə ... as in (20) and (21).
ʔukʷaxʷatᵊb ʔə tsi dsqa ʔə ti sut̓əqalikʷ ʔə tsiʔiɬ sk̓ʷuyčəɬ.
gloss: My older sister helped our mother make (bread). (My older sister helped with the bread-making of our mother.)

form: ʔušudub ʔə tə sqʷəbayʔ ʔə ti suʔigʷəɬ ʔə ti x̌aʔx̌əlus.
gloss: A dog saw a raccoon climb (a tree). (A dog saw the climbing of a raccoon.)

form: Sentence (9) can be expanded with this type of subordinate clause giving (22):
ʔukʷaxʷatᵊb ʔə tsi dsqa tsiʔiɬ sk̓ʷuyčəɬ ʔə ti sut̓əqalikʷs.
gloss: My older sister helped our mother make (bread). (My older sister helped our mother with her bread-making.)

form: Sentences (20) and (22) are synonymous, but in (20) tsiʔiɬ sk̓ʷuyčəɬ our mother is patient in the independent clause while it is agent of the subordinate clause in (22).

In most situations t̓əqalikʷ refers to making bread. (Literally, it means patterned or organized plastering, stroking - note st̓əqxʷ beaver, the animal that plasters its home with its tail.) Nevertheless, there are times when, either for clarity or style, we choose to mention səpləl bread (or flour) specifically as in sentence (8). Including mention of tə səpləl in (22) gives the following:
ʔukʷaxʷatᵊb ʔə tsi dsqa tsiʔiɬ sk̓ʷuyčəɬ ʔə ti sut̓əqalikʷs ʔə tə səpləl.
gloss: My older sister helped our mother make bread.

form: Contrasting (23) with (20) and (18) provides the explanation needed for the problem raised concerning the presence of -s in (2) and its absence in (1). (Subordinate clauses with dəxʷ- and s- pattern identically.)
... ti sut̓əqalikʷs.
gloss: agent

form: ... ti sut̓əqalikʷ ʔə tsiʔiɬ sk̓ʷuyčəɬ.
gloss: agent

form: ... ti sut̓əqalikʷs ʔə tə səpləl.
gloss: agent, patient

form: The ʔə phrases are different; even though they look the same, they represent a different grammatical facet of the language. In (1) there is no agent of the verb in the subordinate clause, dəxʷx̌əbil so (they) become heavy; and ʔə tiʔəʔ this (these opponents in this case) is patient as in II. In (2) there is an agent expressed by -s as in VI and the following ʔə phrase is another subordinate clause expressing manner. It is treated grammatically much like II. (The -ad of gʷəƛ̓əlad stop is not a transitive suffix inspite of its similar shape to a large class of transitives.)
... dəxʷgʷəƛ̓əlads ʔə tiʔəʔ sudᶻigʷicuts.
gloss: ... so they (-s) would stop their (-s) swaying back and forth.

form: ... ti sut̓əqalikʷs ʔə tə səpləl.
gloss: ... her (-s) baking bread.

form: While it would seem easier to learn the single word ʔə in place of a variety of terms like for, with, of, by, etc. as in English, the many uses of ʔə constructions prove instead to be a stumbling block around which the teacher must carefully guide the student.
